analysis.one_liner: Replaces federal income and payroll taxes with a 20 percent value added tax, with rebates for low incomes and a surtax on high incomes.
analysis.headline: The bill — which would have scrapped income and Social Security/Medicare taxes in favor of a 20% value added tax — died in the House Ways and Means Committee with zero cosponsors and never received a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have repealed the federal individual income tax, the corporate income tax, and the Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, and replaced them with a 20 percent tax on the value businesses add — a tax that would show up in the prices of nearly everything people buy. To keep the change from shifting the tax burden onto ordinary families, it pairs the new tax with cash rebates for people with low incomes and a 17 percent surtax on income above $75,000, including profits that owners of closely held corporations keep inside their companies. It was a single senator... rather, a single House member's proposal, introduced late in a congressional session, and it never moved an inch.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, workers would stop paying the payroll taxes taken out of every paycheck to fund Social Security and Medicare; low- and moderate-income people would get a rebate worth up to 20 percent of income up to $30,000, phasing out as income rises; and exporters would gain because goods sold abroad would be exempt while imports would be taxed, a standard feature of value added taxes abroad.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the individual and corporate income taxes and the Federal Insurance Contributions Act (Social Security and Medicare payroll) taxes, effective for years and wages after December 31, 1997.

Provides an annual rebate to eligible individuals with adjusted net income at or below $30,000, worth up to 20 percent of that income and phasing out as income rises, designed to offset the new tax for people least able to pay it.

Imposes a 17 percent assessment on each individual's net income above a $75,000 threshold, and requires owners of closely held C corporations and certain service businesses to treat the company's undistributed profits as personal income, so high earners and business owners do not escape the burden shift.
Excludes exports from the tax and imposes the tax on nonbusiness imports, which the bill's stated principles describe as promoting the competitiveness of American companies in international markets.
Dedicates a portion of the new tax's revenue to the Social Security and Medicare trust funds to keep them in the same financial position they would have been in without the payroll tax repeal.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers would bear the 20 percent tax as it is built into prices across the economy, since businesses pass their tax on in what they charge. People earning above $75,000 would owe a new 17 percent assessment on the excess, and owners of closely held corporations would owe tax on profits the company does not distribute. Businesses would bear the cost of computing, collecting, and remitting the tax on their value added.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers, high earners, and business owners

drawbacks.text: A value added tax applies to consumption, and consumption takes a larger share of a low-income family's budget than a wealthy family's; the rebate is meant to fix this, but it must be claimed annually (though the bill directs that it be delivered with benefits and paychecks where practical), so some eligible people would likely miss out.

The 20 percent rate and the rebate and surtax formulas are labeled tentative; the bill instructs the Treasury Secretary to adjust them within 90 days of enactment to keep the change revenue-neutral and distributionally neutral, so the real burden on any household would not be knowable in advance.

The transition would be enormous: the current income tax apparatus would be dismantled and an entirely new collection system built on business self-reporting, and households that saved under the old income tax would pay the consumption tax again on what they spend.

Ending dedicated payroll contributions and replacing them with a general consumption tax funneled into the trust funds could weaken the traditional link between what workers pay in and what they are promised from Social Security and Medicare.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a serious, carefully drafted attempt at a big trade: workers and businesses would stop paying income and payroll taxes, prices would rise by roughly the amount of the new tax, and the rebate-plus-surtax machinery is designed to leave the overall distribution of the tax burden unchanged. For most working households the swap is roughly a wash by design — a paycheck gain offset by higher prices. The real risks are in the execution: a 20 percent consumption tax is only fair if the rebates reliably reach low-income people and the high-income assessment holds, and rebuilding the entire federal revenue system in one step is the kind of transition that historically produces winners and losers nobody predicted. The bill acknowledges this by making its own numbers tentative pending a Treasury review.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 1996, sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, which kills any bill that has not passed.

narrative.text: Rep. Sam Gibbons introduced the Revenue Restructuring Act of 1996 in the House on September 11, 1996, late in the second session of the 104th Congress.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor.
The complete action history shows only introduction, sponsor remarks, and committee referral — no hearings, no committee vote, and no floor action.
The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the bill expired without ever leaving committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the existing tax system stayed in place. High-income households and owners of closely held corporations, who would have faced the new 17 percent assessment on income above $75,000 and taxation of undistributed corporate profits, were better off that it died; the tax-preparation industry kept its market; and workers kept paying Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes that the bill would have repealed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners, closely held business owners, and tax preparers

for.name: Rep. Sam Gibbons
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee

against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no cosponsors signed on, so the partisan shape of support and opposition was never tested; the bill died quietly in a committee controlled by the opposing party.

industries.note: The bill exempts export sales from the new tax and taxes imports instead, the same border adjustment used by value added taxes worldwide. This is pitched as helping American companies compete abroad, a benefit shared with the domestic workers those industries employ.

industries.industry: High-income households and owners of closely held corporations
industries.note: The bill imposes a 17 percent assessment on net income above $75,000 and forces owners of closely held C corporations and personal-service businesses to count undistributed company profits as personal income. Their gain under the status quo is the revenue the bill would redirect to fund the low-income rebates.

The bill taxes lending, insurance, and dealer services through estimated implicit fees rather than visible receipts, a technical compromise, and requires financial firms to report allocated fees to customers. Banks and insurers avoid some exposure that a pure sales tax on financial flows would create but take on new compliance and reporting work.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: Repealing the individual income tax would eliminate the annual filing burden that the tax-preparation industry's revenue depends on, a cost to the industry that the bill's sponsors counted as a benefit of simplification for ordinary filers.
